**Hydrogen (H₂)** – the most abundant element in the universe – has a rich set of physical, chemical, and nuclear properties. Below is a consolidated overview that covers the key characteristics most commonly referenced in chemistry, physics, and engineering. | Category | Property | Value / Description | |----------|----------|---------------------| | **Basic Atomic Data** | Atomic number | 1 | | | Atomic mass (average) | 1.008 u | | | Standard molar mass | 2.016 g mol⁻¹ (for H₂) | | | Electron configuration | 1s¹ | | | Isotopes | H‑1 (protium), H‑2 (deuterium), H‑3 (tritium) | | | Natural abundance | 99.98 % protium, 0.02 % deuterium, trace tritium | | | Ionization energy (first) | 13.598 eV | | | Electron affinity | –0.754 eV (negative, so H⁻ is unstable) | | | Electronegativity (Pauling) | 2.20 | | **Physical State (Room Temperature)** | State | Gas | | | Color | Colorless | | | Odor | Odorless | | | Taste | Tasteless | | | Density (at 0 °C, 1 atm) | 0.08988 g cm⁻³ | | | Molar volume (at 0 °C, 1 atm) | 22.414 L mol⁻¹ | | | Boiling point | –252.87 °C (121 K) | | | Melting point | –259.16 °C (14 K) | | | Specific heat (Cp) | 28.836 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹ (at 298 K) | | | Heat of vaporization | 0.452 kJ mol⁻¹ | | | Speed of sound in H₂ | ~ 1,200 m s⁻¹ (at 20 °C) | | | Refractive index (visible) | ~1.00013 | | | Viscosity (at 20 °C) | 8.76 µPa·s | | | Thermal conductivity (at 20 °C) | 0.180 W m⁻¹ K⁻¹ | | **Spectroscopic & Quantum Data** | Bond length (H₂) | 0.741 Å | | | Vibrational frequency (ν̃) | 4401 cm⁻¹ | | | Rotational constant (B₀) | 44.594 cm⁻¹ | | | Dissociation energy (D₀) | 4.478 eV (107.5 kJ mol⁻¹) | | | Ionization potential (H₂⁺) | 15.4 eV | | **Chemical Properties** | Reactivity | Highly reactive; forms H₂O, hydrocarbons, metal hydrides | | | Combustion reaction | 2 H₂ + O₂ → 2 H₂O (ΔH° = –286 kJ mol⁻¹) | | | Standard enthalpy of formation (ΔHf°) | 0 kJ mol⁻¹ (elementary state) | | | Standard Gibbs free energy of formation (ΔGf°) | 0 kJ mol⁻¹ | | | Standard entropy (S°) | 130.68 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹ | | | Standard molar heat capacity (Cp°) | 28.836 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹ | | | Solubility in water | 1.6 × 10⁻⁴ mol L⁻¹ (at 25 °C) | | | Solubility in ethanol | ~0.1 mol L⁻¹ | | | pKa of H₂O (as acid) | –1.7 (very weak acid) | | | pKa of H₂ (as base) | –7.0 (very weak base) | | | Redox potential (H₂/H⁺) | 0 V (vs SHE) | | | Oxidation states | +1 (hydride), –1 (hydride ion) | | | Typical reactions | • Combustion → H₂O
• Hydrogenation of alkenes
• Formation of metal hydrides (e.g., NaH, LiH)
• Formation of acids (e.g., HCl, H₂SO₄) | | **Isotopic Variants** | Deuterium (²H) | Mass 2.014 u; heavier, lower zero‑point energy; used in NMR, neutron moderation | | | Tritium (³H) | Mass 3.016 u; radioactive (β⁻ decay, t½ ≈ 12.32 y); used in radiolabeling, fusion research | | | Deuterium oxide (D₂O) | Heavy water; higher boiling/melting points, higher density | | | Tritium oxide (T₂O) | Radioactive water; used in tracer studies | | **Safety & Handling** | Flammability | Extremely flammable; explosive limits 4–75 % (v/v) in air | | | Explosion risk | High; requires proper ventilation and spark‑free equipment | | | Toxicity | Low acute toxicity; inhalation can cause irritation | | | Environmental impact | Minor; contributes to greenhouse effect when released as H₂O vapor | | | Storage | Requires high‑pressure cylinders (up to 700 bar) or cryogenic tanks (liquid H₂ at –253 °C) | | | Regulatory classification | Classified as a hazardous material (flammable gas) under OSHA, DOT, and IATA | | **Applications** | Energy carrier | Fuel cells (PEMFC, SOFC), hydrogen combustion engines | | | Chemical feedstock | Production of ammonia (Haber–Bosch), methanol, hydrogen peroxide | | | Metallurgy | Reduction of metal oxides, hydrogen embrittlement studies | | | Space & aerospace | Propellant for rockets (LH₂/LOX), cooling systems | | | Research | Spectroscopy, quantum chemistry, fusion (ITER), neutron moderation | | | Food & beverage | Hydrogenation of oils, sterilization, flavor masking | | **Astrophysical & Cosmological Role** | Primordial nucleosynthesis | First element formed after Big Bang; ~75 % of baryonic mass | | | Stellar fusion | Core of stars; proton‑proton chain, CNO cycle | | | Interstellar medium | H₂ clouds; sites of star formation | | | Cosmic background radiation | Hydrogen recombination epoch (z≈1100) | --- ### Quick Reference Cheat Sheet | Property | Value | |----------|-------| | **Atomic number** | 1 | | **Molar mass (H₂)** | 2.016 g mol⁻¹ | | **Density (0 °C, 1 atm)** | 0.0899 g cm⁻³ | | **Boiling point** | –252.9 °C | | **Melting point** | –259.2 °C | | **Ionization energy** | 13.6 eV | | **Bond length** | 0.741 Å | | **Dissociation energy** | 107.5 kJ mol⁻¹ | | **Combustion enthalpy** | –286 kJ mol⁻¹ | | **Flammability limits** | 4–75 % (v/v) in air | | **Isotopes** | H‑1, H‑2 (deuterium), H‑3 (tritium) | --- #### Notes & Tips - **Hydrogen’s low density** makes it useful as a lifting gas (though helium is preferred for balloons due to non‑flammability). - **Deuterium** is often used as a tracer in metabolic studies because it can be detected by NMR without altering the chemistry significantly. - **Tritium** is a beta emitter; its handling requires strict radiation safety protocols. - **Fuel cells** convert chemical energy directly to electricity with high efficiency and only water as a by‑product, making hydrogen a clean energy vector. - **Hydrogen embrittlement** is a critical concern in high‑strength steels; understanding H diffusion and trapping is essential for materials engineering. Feel free to ask if you’d like deeper details on any specific property, such as thermodynamic data, spectroscopic constants, or industrial processes involving hydrogen!
